result:
Not quite. "More agents always give better results" is the premise to drop, so the real question isn't five versus ten. It's whether you need to split at all.

Here's a student asking "Can I book the laser cutter tomorrow at 3?" With one agent, the flow is:

1. It checks the calendar.
2. It books the slot.
3. It replies.

That's about 3 model calls. Split it into a "router" agent, a "calendar" agent, a "booking" agent and a "reply" agent, and each hand-off is another model call. Each one re-reads the context it was given, and details can get lost between agents. The same request might now take 8 or more calls, so it costs more and has more places to go wrong. With ten agents it gets worse.

Splitting pays off when the tasks really are different. Examples are a huge manual-search job that would flood one agent's context, or work that can run in parallel. Checking a calendar and booking a slot don't qualify.

Your budget is small, so I'd start with one agent and good tools. Make the steps that are always the same, like the booking confirmation, a fixed workflow. Split only when you can point to a specific problem that splitting solves. That's also the argument that will hold up at your design review.

Quick check: which part of your assistant could you defend splitting out, and what problem would the split solve?
